captions.text: Long ago, signs asked people to protect one rare Florida bird.
The snail kite eats almost nothing but apple snails.
And the snails? Look under the water.
They eat this brown mat, called periphyton.
Anhingas spear fish. Alligators eat fish, turtles, and birds.
Every living thing here is connected.
If one animal disappeared from the Everglades, what would happen to everything else?

words: A diagram showing how energy moves between many connected living things: who eats whom in an ecosystem.
A plant or alga that makes its own food using sunlight, water, and air. Sawgrass and periphyton are producers in the Everglades.
An animal that gets energy by eating other living things. Consumers cannot make their own food.
An animal that hunts and eats other animals. The anhinga is a predator: it dives underwater to spear fish.
An animal that is hunted and eaten by a predator. An apple snail in the water is prey.
A fungus or bacterium that breaks down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil and water.
A spongy mat of algae and tiny living things that grows in Everglades water. It is a producer.

parts.title: Energy Flows Through a Food Web
parts.html:
Every living thing needs energy. In the Everglades, energy starts with the Sun. Producers, like sawgrass and periphyton, use sunlight, water, and air to make their own food.

Consumers can't make food. They get energy by eating producers or other animals. All the eating links together make a food web.

parts.title: Who Eats Whom in the Everglades
parts.html:
Apple snails graze on periphyton, and tiny mosquitofish eat algae and tiny bugs. Snail kites eat apple snails, and anhingas spear small fish. At the top, the alligator eats fish, turtles, and birds.

When anything dies, decomposers like fungi and bacteria break it down and return nutrients to the water.

parts.title: A Model of the Web
parts.html:
Scientists use a food web as a model. It helps them understand how energy moves and predict what happens when something changes.

If one animal disappears, the animals that eat it can go hungry, and the living things it ate can grow out of control.

wall.rule: Energy flows up the tower. It starts with producers and moves up to the top predator. Decomposers break down living things from every level when they die and return nutrients to the water.

mix.q: Sam says, "Alligators are at the top, so they don't matter to the rest of the food web." What do you think?

options.t: Sam is right. Top predators don't change anything.
options.miss: Think about what alligators eat, and about their ponds in the dry season.

options.t: They do matter. Alligators eat other animals, and their ponds hold water and fish in the dry season.
options.ok: Yes! A top predator changes how many animals live below it, and alligator ponds help many animals survive.

wow.title: The Snail Kite Comeback
wow.alt: A dark snail kite flying low over green marsh grass
wow.caption: A male snail kite at Lake Okeechobee, Florida
wow.html:
By the 1960s, only a few dozen snail kites were left in Florida. Many marshes had been drained, so there were few apple snails to eat.

People protected the birds and their marshes, and today Florida has many more snail kites. They still need apple snails to survive.
wow.insetCap: A male snail kite perched in Florida.

keyIdea: In a food web, every living thing is connected. Energy starts with the Sun. Producers use sunlight, water, and air to make their own food, and energy flows up through consumers to the top predator. Decomposers return nutrients at every level. A food web is a model that scientists use to predict what happens when one species disappears.

quiz.q: In a food web diagram, what does an arrow show?

options.t: The path energy takes, from the organism being eaten to the organism eating it
options.ok: 🌿 Exactly right! The arrow follows the energy: it points from prey to predator, showing which way energy flows through the web.

options.miss: Think about it this way: in a food web, something is always getting eaten and something is doing the eating. The arrow shows where the energy goes, from the eaten to the eater. Try again!

options.t: How fast an animal can move
options.miss: Think about it this way: in a food web, something is always getting eaten and something is doing the eating. The arrow shows where the energy goes, from the eaten to the eater. Try again!

quiz.q: Sawgrass is a producer. What does that mean?

options.t: It eats fish and small animals
options.miss: Remember: producers don't eat. They make their own food. Think about what plants do with sunlight. Which answer fits that idea?

options.t: It makes its own food using energy from sunlight
options.ok: 🌱 That's it! Producers are at the base of every food web. They are the only living things that can capture energy from the Sun and turn it into food.

options.t: It breaks down dead organisms in the marsh
options.miss: Remember: producers don't eat. They make their own food. Think about what plants do with sunlight. Which answer fits that idea?

quiz.q: Apple snails disappeared from part of the Everglades. What would most likely happen to the snail kite population?

options.t: Snail kites would struggle to survive, because apple snails are almost their only food
options.ok: ⭐ Right! The snail kite depends on almost one food source. When apple snails are gone, snail kites go hungry. Scientists saw this during a drought in 2007.

options.t: Snail kites would do fine. They would just eat more sawgrass.
options.miss: Think about what the snail kite eats. It's very specific, and that's a big clue. Which answer matches an animal with only one food source?

options.t: Nothing would change. Snail kites don't need food.
